candidato.titulo: A precision T-cell therapy stalls treatment-resistant cancers in clinical trial
candidato.resumo: Experimental drug invika halts progression of refractory tumors by selectively stimulating tumor-fighting T cells.

texto_fonte:
A precision T-cell therapy stalls treatment-resistant cancers in clinical trial
Friday, October 23, 2026
A precision T-cell therapy stalls treatment-resistant cancers in clinical trial
Experimental drug invika halts progression of refractory tumors by selectively stimulating tumor-fighting T cells.
Early results of the first clinical trial to evaluate the drug invikafusp alfa (invika) in humans indicate that the pioneering treatment may be capable of managing cancers that have rebuffed most other interventions, including standard immunotherapy. A study led by researchers at the National Institutes of Health (NIH), Mass General Brigham and Memorial Sloan Kettering found that, at optimal doses, invika was well tolerated and, in patients whose solid tumors had resisted standard immunotherapy, halted disease progression in most and shrank tumors in some.
“Patients whose tumors are advanced — particularly tumors that don’t respond well to immunotherapy — often have their backs against a wall. Few options remain once you reach that point, but these results highlight a more precise means of stimulating anti-tumor immunity that could provide another solution,” said co-corresponding author James Gulley, M.D., Ph.D., clinical director at the Center for Cancer Research (CCR), part of NIH’s National Cancer Institute (NCI).
While immunotherapies have already transformed treatment for several cancers, many patients benefit from them for only a short time, or not at all. Tumors frequently adapt to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapies, such as pembrolizumab, limiting long-term benefits. Other strategies aim to rally T cells, the frontline soldiers of adaptive immunity, but usually do so indiscriminately, commonly leading to severe side effects.
Scientists designed the protein invika to engage a small subset of T cells, two groups of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes specifically. By activating only this narrow population rather than T cells broadly, invika is designed to drive anti-tumor activity while avoiding the severe side effects that less selective approaches can cause. Preclinical studies also conducted at CCR indicate that the drug hits its intended marks and stimulates anti-tumor activity in animal models. This new study describes the next step for invika, detailing the results of phase 1 and initial phase 2 experiments in humans.
The researchers leading the trial recruited patients with a wide variety of cancers, the majority of which had not responded well to ICB. In phase 1, they treated study participants with varying dosages of invika every two weeks to evaluate the drug’s safety and determine the optimal dose. While several participants experienced flu-like side effects, these were expected and generally manageable with additional medication and supportive care. After identifying the lowest dose at which desired effects peaked, the researchers advanced to phase 2, treating participants at this optimal dose.
Of the 27 participants treated with the optimal dose across both phases, disease did not progress in 16 (59.3%) of them. Four (14.8%) participants experienced greater than 30% decreases in the size of targeted tumors, two of whom had metastatic colorectal cancer with tumors of a notoriously treatment-resistant type and were receiving invika as their seventh-line therapy. Another responsive participant had stage 4 non-small cell lung cancer, again with tumors that had repelled multiple therapies including ICB. In participants receiving non-optimal levels, invika did not appear to have significant benefit.
In these patients, the study authors found that the drug fostered growth in the target T-cell populations without affecting any other T cells. They linked the four instances of tumor reduction to the largest shifts in target populations, though, as the authors expected at this early stage, immune activity alone did not always produce a measurable clinical response.
“These results are early, and although signs of immune activity don't always translate into benefit to patients at this stage, it is new and exciting to see activity in patients whose cancers had stopped responding to immunotherapy — a group of people with very few options left,” said co-first author Nicholas Tschernia, M.D., a physician-scientist early investigator in the CCR at NCI. “These findings give us a reason to keep studying this new type of immunotherapy, particularly by combining it with other cancer treatments to continue to seek improved results.”
The treatment sponsor, Marengo Therapeutics, previously announced that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted a Fast Track designation to invika to accelerate its evaluation as a treatment for antigen-rich, metastatic colorectal cancer. More recently, FDA has granted the same designation to invika for similar solid tumors, regardless of tissue type, following prior therapy including checkpoint inhibitors.
The ongoing clinical trial is still seeking study participants. Patients interested in enrolling in this study may contact NCI’s toll-free number 1-800-4-Cancer (1-800-422-6237) (TTY: 1-800-332-8615) or email [email protected]. More information can also be found at https://www.cancer.gov/research/participate/clinical-trials-search.
About the National Cancer Institute (NCI): NCI leads the National Cancer Program and NIH’s efforts to dramatically reduce the prevalence of cancer and improve the lives of cancer patients and their families, through research into prevention and cancer biology, the development of new interventions, and the training and mentoring of new researchers. NCI’s intramural research program at the Center for Cancer Research (CCR) conducts innovative, transdisciplinary basic, translational, and clinical studies, including research at the NIH Clinical Center — the world’s largest research hospital. Learn more about the intramural research done in NCI’s CCR. For more information about cancer, please visit the NCI website at www.cancer.gov or call NCI’s contact center, the Cancer Information Service, at 1-800-4-CANCER (1-800-422-6237).
About the National Institutes of Health (NIH): NIH, the nation's medical research agency, includes 27 Institutes and Centers and is a component of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. NIH is the primary federal agency conducting and supporting basic, clinical, and translational medical research, and is investigating the causes, treatments, and cures for both common and rare diseases. For more information about NIH and its programs, visit www.nih.gov.
NIH…Turning Discovery Into Health®

candidato.titulo: Giant virus yields potassium channel gene that illuminates complex protein evolution
candidato.resumo: Researchers have discovered a gene for a tandem potassium channel in an algal virus. The finding supports the view that giant viruses may have contributed significantly to the evolution of complex proteins. The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

texto_fonte:
Giant virus yields potassium channel gene that illuminates complex protein evolution
Researchers have discovered a gene for a tandem potassium channel in an algal virus. The finding supports the view that giant viruses may have contributed significantly to the evolution of complex proteins. The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
So-called tandem potassium channels perform important functions in human physiology. Because they can conduct potassium ions (K+) across the cell membrane, they help, among other things, to stabilize the membrane potential and thereby regulate the electrical excitability of nerve cells.
Structurally, they differ from all other potassium channels in that two of their four pore-forming subunits are directly linked to each other. It is this tandem-like linkage of the subunits that gives them their name.
Unlike every other type of potassium channel, precursors of tandem potassium channels have not been found in bacteria, which has raised questions about their evolutionary origin.
An algal virus carries the channel
In the PNAS article, the international team, including researchers from the Department of Biology at TU Darmstadt and the Department of Natural Sciences at Bonn-Rhein-Sieg University of Applied Sciences (H-BRS), reports on a DNA virus that infects marine algae and whose genome contains a gene for a tandem potassium channel.
"Our experiments show that this gene encodes a protein with the functional properties of a potassium channel," says Dr. Oliver Rauh, a scientist in the DFG research network "CytoTransport" at H-BRS.
Evidence points to viral origins
The authors of the study also examined the evolutionary relationships between the newly discovered viral channel and known tandem potassium channels and made a striking discovery: Contrary to what is assumed for most viral genes, the newly discovered potassium channel gene did not end up in the viral genome by being stolen from the host's genetic material. Rather, the gene appears to be of viral origin.
"This finding further reinforces a new perspective according to which the giant mimiviruses, to which this virus belongs, have played a central role in the evolution of proteins in higher organisms," emphasizes Gerhard Thiel, a professor in the Department of Biology at TU Darmstadt.
The results of the study also underline that these viruses are rich sources of interesting proteins. In the same virus, other researchers have already discovered a light-controlled ion channel that is used in optogenetics, a field recently recognized with the Nobel Prize.
Publication details
Oliver Rauh et al., A functional two-pore-domain K+ channel from a large DNA virus, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (2026). DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2626158123

candidato.titulo: 28 Zero-Day Findings in Less Than Two Days: What AI-Speed Discovery Means for Robotics
candidato.resumo: VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. The post 28 Zero-Day Findings in Less Than Two Days: What AI-Speed Discovery Means for Robotics appeared first on The Robot Report .

texto_fonte:
VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others.
Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers.
Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots.
These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster, and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations.
What AI changes about vulnerability discovery
Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities.
When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change.
Where the findings sit across the robot lifecycle
VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled.
The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage.
- Development and training: Hidden changes can reach the finished robot
A team downloads a pretrained model to adapt for its robot. Loading a malicious file could give an attacker access to the training system, allowing changes to training data or the model itself. A manipulated model could behave normally during routine testing but respond incorrectly to a particular object, scene, or command after deployment. The risk can enter through a tool the team trusts, before anyone attacks the robot directly.
- Simulation and validation: A passing test could give false confidence
Importing a compromised scene or robot model could give an attacker access to the simulation environment. With sufficient control, the attacker could alter simulated sensor readings, physical conditions, or test results. A robot could then appear to pass tests that should have exposed unsafe behavior, leading the team to approve it for real-world use on the basis of misleading evidence.
- Deployment and runtime: Operators could lose visibility or control
An attacker could exploit weaknesses to change files that influence motion planning or send malicious map data that crashes the operator’s monitoring display. Compromising a remote-operation computer could also put the instructions sent to the robot at risk. Depending on the system and its safeguards, these weaknesses could alter robot movement or leave operators unable to see what is happening and respond promptly.
These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior.
In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised.
A published patch still needs to be proven safe
AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior.
An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined.
Three questions can help teams respond:
- Where do we use the affected software? Include training computers, simulation environments, and deployed robots.
- What could the weakness change? Assess whether it could affect models, test results, operator visibility, or robot behavior.
- How do we verify protection? Confirm that the fix addresses the weakness and that the updated system still operates as intended.
When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared.
From discovery to safer deployment
As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior.
That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation.
Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change.

candidato.titulo: File Mover Express: AWS Releases Open-Source Tool for S3 File Transfers
candidato.resumo: AWS has recently released File Mover Express, an open-source application under the Apache 2.0 license for transferring large files between local systems and Amazon S3. Available for macOS, Windows, and Linux, it supports parallel transfers, automatic performance tuning, retries, pause and resume, and file integrity verification. By Renato Losio

texto_fonte:
AWS has recently released File Mover Express, an open-source application under the Apache 2.0 license for transferring large files between local systems and Amazon S3. Available for macOS, Windows, and Linux, it supports parallel transfers, automatic performance tuning, retries, pause and resume, and file integrity verification.
Designed to "move media to S3 at wire speed," File Mover Express supports auto-tuned parallel transfers, pause and resume, a desktop GUI, a scriptable CLI, and automatic uploads from monitored folders.
The project is primarily developed in Go for its transfer engine and TypeScript with Angular for its graphical interface. It also supports integration with AI assistants through MCP and OIDC-based authentication with identity providers. Provanshu Dey, senior solutions architect at AWS, Asbjorn Kjaer, senior software engineer at AWS, Matthew Muccio, solutions architect at AWS, and Ross Dickson, senior customer solutions manager at AWS, explain:
At the core of File Mover Express is a daemon-based transfer engine that decouples transfers from your desktop session. The daemon can run on the machine of your choice, whether that is your workstation, a server in the data center, or an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance, while you control it from a drag-and-drop graphical user interface (GUI) or a scriptable command line interface (CLI) over an encrypted, password-protected connection.
Media teams regularly transfer terabytes of assets between on-premises storage and the cloud. These transfers often involve tight deadlines and processes that must continue after the initiating user or machine disconnects. Traditional transfer clients may stop when a desktop session ends, while commercial alternatives can introduce licensing costs, proprietary protocols, or third-party infrastructure. File Mover Express supports uploads and downloads, allowing teams to transfer large files to Amazon S3 and retrieve them for editing, review, or restoration.
Source: GitHub project
File Mover Express splits large files into chunks and uploads them in parallel using multipart uploads. With the autotuning mode, it adjusts the number of parallel streams and chunk sizes to optimize throughput for the available connection. Transfers also support configurable retries and file-level pause and resume. Dey, Kjaer, Muccio, and Dickson add:
File Mover Express provides security features including file encryption in flight, file encryption at rest, and encryption for the control plane. All transfers use HTTPS, and access to your S3 buckets is governed by AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) with a documented minimum-permission policy (...) For teams that centralize identity, File Mover Express supports single sign-on through OpenID Connect (OIDC).
File Mover Express calculates checksums in the background and caches them locally for reuse when files remain unchanged. It supports MD5, XXHash, XXHash64, and XXH3, offering a choice between compatibility and hashing performance. For transfers to distant buckets, users can enable S3 Transfer Acceleration, while bandwidth limits help control network usage. On LinkedIn, Dickson writes:
Moving large media files to the cloud shouldn't be the slow part of your day :) That’s why a group of us at AWS built File Mover Express (...) For anyone in media moving camera cards, dailies, or deliverables, it tackles the usual pain.
The project's source code is available on GitHub, along with pre-built packages for macOS, Windows, and Linux.

candidato.titulo: Sam Altman meets with Samsung leadership to secure more RAM for data centers amid crushing shortages
candidato.resumo: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman met with around 50 Samsung executives in South Korea on October 31 to discuss AI's future, business opportunities and the technology's impact on corporate operations. The meeting comes as demand for memory chips grows alongside AI infrastructure spending, putting pressure on global DRAM supplies. Samsung and SK hynix together accounted for approximately 83% of global high-bandwidth memory revenue in the second quarter of 2026, highlighting South Korea's central role in supplying the hardware behind the AI expansion.

texto_fonte:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has met with about 50 senior Samsung executives in South Korea, as the company seeks to expand its Artificial Intelligence and memory capacity, Bloomberg reports. Altman’s visit to South Korea follows his recent comments about how the world's limited memory supply should be allocated. In an interview on the Chick Pink podcast this week, the OpenAI chief argued that DRAM sitting inside personal computers is often underused, describing it as “quite terrible”. He suggested that data centers could make more intensive use of memory by sharing computer resources across AI workloads. The argument has drawn widespread criticism given OpenAI’s own services like ChatGPT rely heavily on centralized computing infrastructure.
The meeting, which took place at Samsung’s Resources Development Center in Yongin on Saturday, October 30, brought together chiefs from the company’s financial, electronics, and biotechnology businesses. Confirming the meeting, Samsung Korea said the discussion revolved around strengthening existing relationships between the two companies, particularly a letter of Intent signed in October 20225 to cooperate on global AI infrastructure, including supplying memory semiconductors for OpenAI’s Stargate project. “The Samsung executives and CEO Sam Altman discussed the direction of AI technology development and its potential applications, as well as new markets and business opportunities that will emerge from it,” Samsung stated.
Samsung, however, emphasized more on AI transformation and future business opportunities, rather than announcing a new memory supply agreement. Reportedly, Altman also presented Samsung’s AI Center head with a Codex Micro Keyboard, a device designed for use with OpenAI’s coding agent. The latest meeting comes as demand from AI centers continues to soar, with AMD forecasting DRAM revenue will jump 177% in 2026 to about $416 billion. Trendforce also estimates DRAM supply will fall 1% to 2% short of demand this year, with the imbalance expected to worsen in 2027. New manufacturing capacity may take time to come, which means the shortage could persist into 2028, as per a recent warning by Micron.
For now, demand for data centers is facing major competition, especially from PCs, smartphones, and other electronics, for limited memory supplies (and may be nowhere close to peaking). High-bandwidth memory (HBM), a specialized form of DRAM used in AI devices, has become particularly important as companies deploy increasingly powerful computing systems.
Samsung and SK Hynix are among the world's leading memory manufacturers, giving South Korea a central role in supplying the hardware behind the AI expansion. According to Counterpoint Research, both companies controlled about 63% of global DRAM revenues in the second quarter of 2026. Their influence is greater in HBM, where the two South Korean manufacturers accounted for roughly 83% of global revenue. This has prompted other technology executives to approach the country, with AMD CEO Lisa Su visiting earlier this month to discuss securing additional HBM supplies from SAMSUNG, saying, "It is important to plan three to five years ahead with our partners."
Meanwhile, Samsung and SK Hynix have been upgrading Chinese factories to meet the surging demand for AI-related memory and storage products. However, those particular upgrades concern NAND flash production, rather than DRAM — but they show just how manufacturers are adjusting capacity as demand shifts towards data center hardware.

Newton Gitonga is a tech journalist covering gadgets, PC hardware, AI, data centers, and the wider tech industry. His interest in technology started early, taking apart things around the house to see how they worked, often to his dad’s frustration. His curiosity sometimes got the better of him, including a few failed attempts to fix laptops, one of them a gifted Dell XPS. He has previously written for Notebookcheck, ZyCrypto, CoinCentral, and Crypto News Flash.

candidato.titulo: Heavy hydrogen in 3I/ATLAS's methane points to a frigid birthplace
candidato.resumo: The interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS carries a chemical clue to conditions in the planetary system of its origin, locked away long before it reached our sun. Its methane signature is unusually rich in heavy hydrogen, suggesting that the comet's frozen ingredients took shape in an intensely cold environment around another star—or in the cloud that preceded it.

texto_fonte:
Heavy hydrogen in 3I/ATLAS's methane points to a frigid birthplace
Andrew Zinin
Author
The interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS carries a chemical clue to conditions in the planetary system of its origin, locked away long before it reached our sun. Its methane signature is unusually rich in heavy hydrogen, suggesting that the comet's frozen ingredients took shape in an intensely cold environment around another star—or in the cloud that preceded it.
Using the James Webb Space Telescope, Nathan Roth of American University and NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center and colleagues measured a heavy-to-ordinary hydrogen ratio in 3I/ATLAS that's about 13 times as high as that of comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko (which likely originated in our own solar system).
Their findings, published in Nature Astronomy, give scientists a rare opportunity to investigate another planetary system's early chemistry. The challenge is working backward from the escaping gas to the conditions that made its ice.
Finding a faint signal between brighter ones
Heavy hydrogen, called deuterium, has an extra neutron in its nucleus. It can take the place of ordinary hydrogen in a molecule of methane, which consists of one carbon atom joined to four hydrogen atoms. That substitution changes the molecule's infrared signature, allowing astronomers to distinguish between the two forms, but the deuterium-bearing version produces a much fainter signal.
Webb observed 3I/ATLAS on Dec. 22 and 23, 2025, when it was about 2.4 times as far from the sun as Earth is. The telescope examined infrared light from the coma, the cloud of gas surrounding the comet's icy nucleus.
The researchers modeled and subtracted light from other gases, then looked between ordinary methane's much brighter features for the faint traces of its heavier counterpart. Those signals yielded a deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio, or D/H ratio, of approximately 3.2% in methane.
"This D/H ratio exceeds any other value for methane measured in the solar system," the authors write.
The comparison with comet 67P, which is a Jupiter-family comet that probably originated in the Kuiper Belt, is especially useful because it is the only other comet in which deuterium-bearing methane has been detected. That measurement required a close-up investigation by the Rosetta spacecraft. Webb detected the molecule from afar in 3I/ATLAS, a visitor born outside our solar system.
What the ice remembers
Why should an extra neutron reveal anything about a comet's birthplace?
In extremely cold gas, some chemical reactions favor the incorporation of deuterium into molecules. At temperatures around 10 degrees above absolute zero, reactions that would undo that enrichment become less effective. Chemical reactions on interstellar dust grains can then build deuterium-rich ice that eventually becomes part of a comet.
The new measurement also adds a clue about timing. Methane's D/H ratio was about three times the ratio previously measured in 3I/ATLAS's water. The researchers suggest that the methane may have formed later, after the surrounding chemistry had had more time to concentrate heavy hydrogen.
The team argues that the methane result fits with the theory of proposed origin for 3I/ATLAS in a cold cloud or an environment surrounding a forming star, with relatively few elements heavier than helium and a high rate of cosmic-ray bombardment. Those energetic particles help start the reactions that enrich molecules in deuterium.
That offers a plausible history rather than a uniquely identified birthplace, however. Direct measurements of methane's D/H ratio in distant star-forming environments for comparison are lacking, and the few chemical models that report such estimates fall short of the value measured here.
The comet therefore gives those models a demanding test. Dense material around young stars can hide the ice chemistry from telescopes, but 3I/ATLAS has carried some of that material within our reach. Any descriptions of how its ingredients formed must now explain why its methane contains so much heavy hydrogen.

candidato.titulo: Julien Camirand Lemire (Nord Quantique): One Cavity, One Error-Corrected Qubit
candidato.resumo: Julien Camirand Lemire, co-founder and CEO of Nord Quantique, is interviewed by Yuval Boger. Julien discusses Nord Quantique‘s bosonic code approach, which uses microwave photons in superconducting cavities to achieve quantum error correction without large qubit overhead, including their GKP and Tesseract code demonstrations and a quantum error correction gain that has more than doubled […]

texto_fonte:
Julien Camirand Lemire, co-founder and CEO of Nord Quantique, is interviewed by Yuval Boger. Julien discusses Nord Quantique‘s bosonic code approach, which uses microwave photons in superconducting cavities to achieve quantum error correction without large qubit overhead, including their GKP and Tesseract code demonstrations and a quantum error correction gain that has more than doubled since 2024. They explore the company’s roadmap toward 10^-7 to 10^-9 error rates by 2032, the four-qubit system entering operation this year, and how Quebec’s Sherbrooke ecosystem has enabled a capital-efficient build. They also discuss high-rate codes, transmon-based scaling challenges, and much more.
Transcript
Yuval: Hello, Julien, thank you for being here.
Julien: Hi, Yuval, it’s a great pleasure to be here with you.
Yuval: So who are you and what do you do?
Julien: So I’m Julien Camirand Lemire, I’m co-founder and CEO of Nord Quantique. W e are a quantum computing hardware company building differentiated technology that really is anchored into error correction for scaling purposes.
Yuval: And you’re in Canada, right? That’s Canada with a Q, I believe.
Julien: Yes, Canada with a Q. We’re in Quebec, Canada, so it’s even more Q in the name. But yeah, we’re based in Sherbrooke, so we have offices here in the Sherbrooke ecosystem that is a pretty strong powerhouse in quantum in Canada, but also have offices in Montreal, which is well-known.
Yuval: So you got me interested in differentiated technology. Please explain.
Julien: Great. Yeah, I think, so we are a spin-off of this Sherbrooke ecosystem, as I’ve been mentioning. So we incorporated the company back in 2020. And at that time, I think it was pretty clear what we wanted to do, which is really build a technology. So a type of qubit that is capable of running quantum error correction. And the reason we were doing this is really looking at what the industry has been doing for the past 10 years. And I think we should just appreciate all the progress we have done as an industry in building quantum computing hardware that is more complex and scaling as well. So meaning that we have now as an industry systems that’s up somewhere between a hundred and thousands of qubits that are becoming more and more available. But despite this great progress, I think there are still some challenges, some very hard challenges that the industry is facing. And one of these challenges is errors as we are aware. So these qubits, they make errors, they’re prone to noise, and we need to deal with this. And the best way that the industry has started to also acknowledge is the need for quantum error correction. So this sort of error management layer that sits into the quantum computing stack that is there to detect and correct errors as they occur during a quantum computation. And the challenge with quantum error correction usually is the fact that it consumes a lot of resources. So you need some form of overhead inside your quantum computers to deal with these errors. So this overhead often comes in the forms of number of qubits. So you need a certain number of qubits more in your quantum computer to get there. And usually this factor is somewhere between 100 to 1,000. So that requires a larger and larger size system. But nothing tells you that this redundancy that is needed by quantum error correction has to come in the form of more qubits. And this is where we approach things a little bit differently at Nord Quantique. So the thing that you need for quantum error correction is a form of redundancy. And what we’re building is a technology that is called bosonic codes. These bosonic codes are made of microwave photons trapped into superconducting resonators. And the great thing about them is that you can trap multiple microwave photons inside a single cavity or single resonator, which provides you with the redundancy you need to do quantum error correction in a single cavity, which is really the embodiment of the hardware we’re building at Nord Quantique. So yeah, this is really what is differentiated about this technology is how we deal with quantum error correction, really trying to lower the overhead, sorry, to achieve quantum error correction in quantum hardware.
Yuval: There are other approaches, right? Amazon is developing a chip. Alice and Bob has a chip that they say will reduce the number of qubits required because I think it only, you know, it de-amplifies one type of error and you have to deal only with the other. How is that different than what you guys are doing?
Julien: Yeah, definitely. So bosonic codes is a large space. I think this just from the quantum perspective, so this is why we like these codes, but also just as the types of qubits we can build with bosonic codes, there’s many of them. Alluding to Alice and Bob who is developing certain types of cat qubit that is, as you’re mentioning, reducing one error channel. In our case, we use a different version that we call grid states. So the most notable example of these grid states is the GKP qubit. So we did some demonstration of that qubit early 2024. I think we’ve released our demonstration there. In these qubits, you can do full quantum error correction on a single of these qubits, so correcting for both X and Z errors, and this is what you will find in our 2024 paper. Beyond this also, these codes can be expanded to what we call multimode codes, so multiple, like in these cavity you can store multiple photons, you can also store photons of different frequencies, and these enables you to run different types of code, like the Tesseract code, which is a different example of the grid state that we have released in 2025.
Yuval: Do these cavities require cooling to near absolute zero, or do you operate at room temperature?
Julien: Yeah, thank you. Yeah, so we’re based on a superconducting platform, so what we use are the same building blocks as any superconducting qubit hardware, so we use resonators, of course. We use Josephson junctions to couple these resonators together and also to control them. So these operate at low temperature. But I think what is differentiated also from our architecture is that we need a smaller cryogenic environment to run systems in the end. So because we save resources for quantum error correction, there’s some layer of scaling that we don’t anticipate having to do. I mean, we’re reducing the overhead for quantum error correction by a large fraction with this cavity. And the purpose is really to build quantum computers, yes, in cryogenic environment, but in a constrained size. So something that will fit into 10 meters squared for more than 2000 of these logical qubits.
Yuval: So to get to real application, one doesn’t need a lot of qubits, just needs a large enough number of good enough qubits. And you’re basically saying that if I wanted a 200 qubit machine using your technology, I would need roughly 200 resonators, right? 200 cavities.
Julien: Yeah, that’s the purpose of the technology. So I think something that is interesting about that technology is you revert also to our paper in 2024. So we are able to do quantum error correction on single cavities. If you look at the performance of that system in 2024, it’s not where we need it to be in terms of real-world applications. So we still need to improve on quantum error correction and so on. The thing that is great about that system is we have a way to do this without increasing the footprint of the system. So this is the multimode code approach that I’ve mentioned. So building better codes in single cavities, for example, is one way to do this, but also we’re improving across the board. So as you’re mentioning, Yuval, so this is really the purpose of this system is really what we’d like to achieve, what we call the one-to-one ratio. So one cavity is an error-corrected qubit and scale the technology with this building block.
Yuval: If we just go into the 2024 paper, was it essentially quantum memory or were you showing quantum operations as in gates?
Julien: Yeah, so this paper in 2024 was a demonstration as a quantum memory. Since then, we have done gates that we presented at different conferences. And in our blog post, for example, in our blog page, you will see also the operation on gate of these qubits.
Yuval: Now you know what the next question is. So when can we see some gates?
Julien: What can we see in this? So we already have demonstrated gates. So you can see this on our webpage. I think the picture I have behind me is also a picture of our four qubit system. So this will be in operation this year and also something that we intend to work with partner to be operating with all these gates, but also working directly with error-corrected qubits. So this is for this year, the first release of that system and more publicly, if I would say.
Yuval: The 2024 demo also used some post-selection, right? Or was it just 100% error correction?
Julien: 100% error correction, yeah. So no post-selection. We also improved on that layer. So at that time, I think there’s one metric that we track internally is the quantum error correction gain. So by which factor are we improving sort of the performance of the hardware with quantum error correction? And now we also more than doubled on that number. So initially it was just barely making it. So I think we had a factor of 1.1 at that time. Now we’re beyond two and keep improving also the quantum error correction capabilities on these codes.
Yuval: Could you explain what that means? So let’s assume that you now, someone will test the four qubit system, maybe have some gates in it. You have built-in error correction. So what’s the gate fidelity? Is it a hundred percent or is it? Three nines, six nines, nine nines. I mean, what are we looking at?
Julien: Yeah, yeah, so we’re looking at, so depending on exactly what we’re looking into, so I think we’re talking around three nines is what we are working with right now in terms of operation on a single cavity and the two qubit, yeah, this is still improving. And also like we are adding the quantum error correction layer on top of all of this. What we think is interesting about this is the fact that we’re running quantum error correction today with these cavities. What it means is also we are improving this quantum error correction layer, but it comes with no surprise after this. I think this is how the system runs. You don’t have these things like post-selection. We’re not compromising on certain gates to allow for certain codes. So it’s the same codes that will be running on these systems. The other piece is also that we don’t have this classical layer that is usually there in quantum error correction to sort of do the syndrome measurement. So all the error correction that we’re running here is done autonomously, which is another differentiator of the quantum operation on that system.
Yuval: Three nines is nice, but certainly not enough. So does this approach take you to, what, a tera quop? How many nines does it take you to, or what do you have to do to get to the finish line?
Julien: Yeah, so I think it’s, so what we have to do is more of the same. So what I’ve mentioned earlier is, of course, the performance of the quantum hardware that we have today is not to reach usefulness. However, what we have unlocked with these cavities is also a way to improve performance with this multimode quantum error correction approach that I’ve mentioned earlier to unlock higher performance. And we have done demonstration of this. So you refer also to post-selection, which is something that we can do with the Tesseract code that enables us also to, which is sort of the two-mode version of the GKP code that I’ve mentioned earlier. And on that cavity, what we’ve shown is that we can operate with similar performance as the GKP code without post-selection, but when we turn that layer on, we’re able to shut an error channel off. And then all of a sudden, the logical performance, so the decay of the logical information, we were not able to measure it at that point, meaning that the decay was extremely low for that experiment. So what I’m saying here is that, yes, we need to improve, but we are improving by building these quantum error correction codes that are built on that artillery of multimode codes inside single cavities. So that’s the path forward for the company. Of course, we’re building bigger systems. That’s one axis of scaling. The other one is just pure quantum error correction improvement, which in each of the cavities that we’re building. And then what are we targeting? So we think we can reach 10 to the minus seven to 10 to the minus nine error rates, which in single cavity with these multiple techniques.
Yuval: When?
Julien: By when, exactly, that’s the right question. So our target for this is around 2032. So this is in terms of error rate, of course, we’re improving from now to then, unlocking these different codes with this.
Yuval: What you’re showing, what you showed in 2024, what you’re telling me now is very impressive. So I’m curious, why does it take six more years to get to what you’re describing? What’s the holdup? Is it you need just more money? Is there algorithmic issues that you have to solve? What is stopping you?
Julien: More money is always welcome, of course. But at the same time, I think this is something we should chat about also. We had a pretty capital efficient approach up to now. We believe also our technology allows for something that is more capital efficient growing from now on. I think some of the challenges that we have faced with bosonic codes also relates to the fact that it’s very different from the rest of the industry. I think a lot of the simulation tools we had to build, how we do quantum error correction for this hardware is also specific to that hardware. And this is part of the things that we have unlocked until now. And from now to the future, I think what we’re building is not only just better qubits, we’re also scaling the technology. So I’ve mentioned trying to achieve also these thousands of logical qubits that we’re aiming for these similar timeline that I’ve just mentioned is part of the journey that gets us there. So yeah, so more scaling, a lot of engineering and integration of this quantum error correction capability into scaled-up systems is what is ahead of us.
Yuval: There’s been a lot of press recently about high-rate codes. You know, Harvard released some results and others. So whereas previously one would imagine that you need a thousand physical qubits to get a good enough logical qubit, maybe the answer is we just need two, for instance. How are you thinking about these publications? Do they encourage you? Do they discourage you? What are your thoughts?
Julien: I think it, like, first of all, it’s impressive. It’s interesting. I think a couple of years back when people were looking at quantum error correction, I think it seems also impossible that we would have that discussion and reducing qubit count to these pairs. I think something that convinced us that the approach is the right one here. It’s also the trade-off between number of qubits and clock rate, we believe is good with the bosonic codes that we have right now. The other piece is also, we don’t need to rebuild the whole architecture for every new code that we’re implementing. As long as we have enough modes in our cavity, this is something that we can do on the fly as well. So no, it doesn’t scare us. I think it just shows progress. I think it shows also the importance of quantum error correction and the work that is needed to be done from an industry perspective.
Yuval: I believe you’ve transitioned from CTO to CEO, you know, a couple of years ago. What have you, how does that change your perspective? What have you done or what has the company done differently since that transition?
Julien: That’s a good, good question. So I think we expanded the leadership team also just to expand our bandwidth as a leadership team. Of course, I do more and more fundraising now, so this is just more of my work. But also, we’re building the company right now and we’re extending in that perspective. That switch of role was really just to enable us to be more scalable in that front. I think we have been successful to that point. So we’re really in a growth phase right now. So scaling the team, scaling the technology, but also just growing as an organization.
Yuval: Beyond fundraising, is there a commercial movement that you’re doing right now? Are you selling access? Are you selling computers? When you have that four qubit machine, how do you expect people to use it?
Julien: Yeah. So right now we are in discussions for a sale of a system. So that will be our first system sale. How we’re thinking about these system sales and just system access in general is we like to work with partners. So we have partners also that are developing applications on these. The machine also that we’re running with four or fewer qubits at the moment, and right now these partners have access also. Working also closely with what we call our application teams that support these external partners accessing the hardware or running any algorithms on these qubits as well. So this is how we also anticipate the next phases for commercial traction. At the same time, I think selling a ton of systems is not something that we will see from Nord. I think what you will see from us is selling more and more of these systems, but at the same time, our goal is really to have commercially viable quantum computers at the right moment. So we’re really aiming for usefulness here, and for us, this goes through unlocking quantum error correction and so on.
Yuval: You’re describing an architecture that is, well, maybe very complex to build, but potentially simple to use, right? And no need for a classical error correction there. Therefore, maybe the programming is rather simple. So what do you expect people to do with a four qubit system? I mean, obviously you can’t do something truly useful. The software sounds like it’s straightforward. What are you hoping to get from initial partners using that four qubit system?
Julien: I think, yeah, you’re right. So we won’t run any useful algorithms on those. Despite the fact that there’s some interesting angles sometimes, also there’s some specific things we can do with our present system that goes a little bit beyond this qubit world and quantum error correction. But I think the first piece is just running algorithms with quantum error correction on it, on top of it, and see how it impacts also the algorithms and so on. So it’s a good benchmark for people just to have access to an error-corrected system and us just to learn how these algorithms get to work with all the artillery in place.
Yuval: You mentioned capital efficiency. Is that by design or just it wasn’t the right time or was difficult to raise money some years ago?
Julien: No, no, no. It’s by design. So yeah, so I’ve mentioned, so we’re a spin-off of the Sherbrooke ecosystem. So there’s a quantum institute there, so it’s called Institut Quantique. So Quebec is a French-speaking nation, so everything is written in French as well. But Institut Quantique is one of the powerhouses also in quantum computing development across Canada, especially when it comes to hardware. So we’re really a spin-off of that environment. That environment also has a lot of history when it comes to microelectronics. So it is part of what we call the Northeastern Semiconductor Manufacturing Corridor that runs all the way down to Albany, ends up here in Sherbrooke and in Bromont, where fabs, but also with strong ties with the microelectronic industry, like plants like IBM packaging plants that is located in Bromont, Teledyne also has a plant there, they build the lens that are responsible for the rover that is on Mars right now. So there’s a lot of this sort of microelectronic industry, which means also that in our ecosystem, there’s a lot of tech transfer happening in this sort of sector. Quebec and Canada have invested a lot of money. In our case, it’s more than a billion of investment that we are leveraging from different pieces of infrastructure. Think of these fabrication facilities that we are using. So we have access to fabs that are also dedicated to superconducting fabrication. And it’s really our team operating this infrastructure on the ground that runs this. But we didn’t have to pay for this. Like, this was there, we’re just renting the access. And that is also true for some of the quantum hardware that we need to access, so fridges, a lot of the benchmarking facilities. So we could rent a lot of this equipment infrastructure. So this is money that we didn’t have to spend. So it really is by design. So the ecosystem in which we are is really embedded into this like tech transfer philosophy. And there’s a lot of infrastructure that was put in place that we were able to leverage. And now of course we’re growing. So that model where we rent a lot of the infrastructure has an end, but at the same time, it ends at the right time. I mean, we’ve done our demonstration and just from a capital perspective, so we’re getting money at the right time to do the right thing. And the second piece for us is really the technology. So the fact that we have this overhead reduction in terms of achieving quantum error correction and so on, means that we have smaller systems to build and this costs less in the end.
Yuval: As we get closer to the end of our discussion today, just a few quick questions. One is if the technology that you’re describing was not available, no bosonic codes, just gone, what modality would you prefer?
Julien: That’s a good question. It’s a tricky one. I think all modalities have sort of advantages and disadvantages. So beyond the bosonic codes, which I think has a really strong interest, especially as it comes to scaling technologies beyond this, we’re still a superconducting platform. The reason we are a superconducting platform is, of course, that’s a technology that was developed for a long time, so we know about it, but also it’s fast. I think that’s also something that we benefit from on the bosonics side. So the technology is fast. We keep that operation rate functioning for our bosonic qubits. And I think this will be important in the end. So I think that that’s a strong axis for superconducting qubits and so on. I do think this more standard transmon-based approach faces some challenges, especially when it comes to like connecting multiple fridges into a network environment. So there’s a lot of technology that needs to be advanced in order for the community to get there. But just if we are able to pass that wall in some sense, the fact that the technology is fast will remain a key advantage there.
Yuval: And as you think about the market evolution over the last couple of years, what has most surprised you?
Julien: I would say that the rate of evolution of the quantum error correction field, I think it’s, it’s impressive seeing, and it was a lot of the different demonstrations, whether it’s superconducting platform, neutral atoms, and now more and more people starting to bring that technology forward, to push for it. And we’re starting to, I think we will soon start to see the benefits of this in systems that will not only be playing with quantum error correction, but really start integrating that technology and scaling forward. Because like in our perspective, this is really one of the critical bricks that is in today’s most advanced systems and we really need to solve this as an industry if we want to have a useful system one day.
Yuval: And last hypothetical, if you could have dinner with one of the quantum greats, dead or alive, who would that be?
Julien: Sorry, say that again?
Yuval: If you could have dinner with one of the quantum greats, dead or alive, who would that be?
Julien: It’s funny because I was just at dinner with Michel Devoret, so Nobel Prize winner today actually, he’s visiting the ecosystem, so I’m pretty sort of on that end here. But, but all but that would have been my pick. Also, I think this Michel is not only somebody with whom we shared strong ties, but also he’s the founder of this demonstration of bosonic codes in superconducting circuits. So.
Yuval: Wonderful. Julien, thank you so much for joining me today.
Julien: Thank you so much, Yuval.
Yuval Boger is the Chief Commercial Officer of QuEra Computing.
Yuval Boger

candidato.titulo: Biwin M560 2TB SSD Review: The DRAM-less drive to beat
candidato.resumo: The Biwin M560 brings SMI’s SM2504XT to retail with top-tier responsiveness and excellent efficiency, though not the fastest post-cache writes.

texto_fonte:
Tom's Hardware Verdict
The Biwin M560 is one of the best all-around PCIe 5.0 SSDs we’ve tested, with class-leading responsiveness and excellent efficiency.
Reasons to buy
- + Top-tier application and gaming performance
- + Low 4KB random read latency
- + Excellent power efficiency
Reasons to avoid
- - No 4TB option
- - Slower writes after the cache fills
Why you can trust Tom's Hardware
Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
We’re back with another drive from Biwin, which has been putting out some good SSDs with minor exceptions. This one uses hardware we’ve wanted to test in retail for quite some time: the SMI SM2504XT SSD controller, which is hard to find. The PCIe 5.0 DRAM-less range is relatively popular because it offers the performance without the power and heat of higher-end options, at a lower price point. The tech’s newer than what PCIe 4.0 drives offer, so you get a better all-around experience if you’re willing to take the plunge. The M560 slots in here perfectly as a real alternative to all the drives in this class with Phison hardware.
Biwin M560 Specifications
The Biwin M560 is available only in 1TB and 2TB capacities. Is that a disappointment? It’s normal to expect at least 4TB SKUs these days, but 8TB is certainly a bridge too far for a four-channel controller. Yes, we have some 8TB DRAM-less drives floating around, but for the most part you can’t find those units. 4TB is more common and highly desired — this is what makes the Lexar NM790 so legendary — but it actually is a decent amount of flash for this type of controller. With the ideal amount of flash for this controller being four dies per channel, or 16 total, 2TB really is the sweet spot. So we’re fine with that for this drive, even if it is higher-end.
Right now the drive can be found for $189.99 and $364.99 for the two SKUs, which is not unreasonably priced for the hardware. At 2TB, it is right in line with the Crucial P510, for example. It’s also below the top drives with DRAM, like the Samsung 9100 Pro, by enough that it makes sense. You can get PCIe 5.0 DRAM SSDs at around this price or cheaper, but you’re giving up some things to do so, which we’ll get into later.
The drive is rated for up to 11,000 / 10,000 MB/s for sequential reads and writes and up to a whopping 1,700K / 1,700K random read and write IOPS. 1.7 million IOPS! That’s astounding, and even exceeds the 1.3+ million, on paper, from direct competitor Phison E31T-based drives, like the Corsair MP700 Elite. This thing is a beast for a DRAM-less drive.
Biwin doesn’t skimp on the warranty, either. It’s the typical five-year affair for duration, but you’re covered for up to 750TB of writes for every TB of space. This is 25% more than is typical, if you care about that sort of thing. We consider it a bonus.
Biwin M560 Software and Accessories
Hitting the download tab for the M560’s site shows three downloads available: the Biwin Data Recovery Tool for macOS, one for Windows, and Biwin Intelligence. The first two are pretty self-explanatory, but we will give kudos to Biwin for having the macOS option. For the last, it is the company’s SSD toolbox, which is an all-in-one software solution dashboard you can use to check your drive’s health, update firmware, and so forth. Biwin lists the supported functions on its page. The toolbox only supports Windows at this time.
Biwin M560: A Closer Look
The Biwin M560 is, as expected, a single-sided drive, which we prefer. Less that can go wrong, fits into more machines, and can be easier to cool. The top label is heat-spreading. The back label has drive information, including the 3.3 V / 2.0 A rating, which puts the drive power draw below about 7W. According to the S.M.A.R.T. report, the maximum power draw is 8W.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
These numbers might be concerning, especially as good DRAM-less SSDs tend to be at around 6.5W or less. Well, as it turns out, the drive is much more comfortable at 4W, with a maximum significantly below 6.5W and an average of one-half that, as you can explore in more detail with our power testing. Even very efficient PCIe 5.0 drives tend to step up over the last generation, making heat something to watch in some cases. Not in this one — we think this will be great in laptops, and exceptionally cool in PCIe 4.0 ones.
The components don’t even take up half of the PCB space! Impressive engineering, and the extra spacing between components can help spread heat. Here we have one controller, the SMI SM2504XT, which we previously covered in an ES preview, and two NAND flash packages. The controller performed exceptionally in our preview testing and is more than a match for the best controllers out there, whether Phison’s competing E31T or even many drives with DRAM such as those based on the E26. The flash, in this case, is Kioxia’s 218-layer BiCS8 TLC, which is also exceptional. This flash has excellent latency and is also power-efficient. This combination is a match made in heaven, and it’s a shame we don’t see the SM2504XT more often.

texto_fonte:
Microsoft prepara "arma secreta" para receber GTA 6 no XBOX Series
Por Gabriel Cavalheiro • Editado por Jones Oliveira |
O lançamento de GTA 6 está cada vez mais próximo. O PlayStation 5, uma das plataformas de lançamento do jogo, não tem só uma vantagem em unidades vendidas, como também uma parceria de marketing com a Rockstar Games que o deixa alguns quilômetros à frente do rival XBOX Series.
Prova disso é que dados da Sensor Tower mostram a vantagem gigantesca do console da Sony em relação ao console da Microsoft na pré-venda de GTA 6. Somado a isso, o trailer final do jogo cravou que “a melhor experiência é no PS5”.
No entanto, o que ninguém esperava era que o XBOX prepararia uma "arma secreta" para receber o grande jogo da Rockstar. Em outubro, a marca anunciou que os consoles e dispositivos XBOX ganhariam upscaling com IA da AMD para disputar com o PlayStation e a Nintendo.
Trata-se do FSR 4.1, que promete ganhos gráficos e de performance via Inteligência Artificial e estará disponível no XBOX Series e nos modelos ROG XBOX Ally X e X25. Será que a divisão de games do XBOX terá alguma vantagem no lançamento de GTA 6?
GTA 6 pode rodar bem no XBOX Series S
GTA 6 chegará ao PlayStation 5 e ao XBOX Series em 19 de novembro de 2026. Desde o anúncio do jogo e das plataformas, muitos jogadores se perguntam se haverá GTA 6 para o XBOX Series S, console de entrada da atual geração.
O hardware, apelidado de 'monstrinho' por fãs e de 'atraso' por outros, ficou marcado por polêmicas relacionadas à sua potência inferior à do XBOX Series X e do PS5 para rodar jogos, o que rende discussões até hoje.
Isso pode mudar totalmente de figura com a adição do FSR 4.1, que promete transformar o Series S em uma verdadeira máquina. Vale lembrar que o Nintendo Switch 2 também possui uma tecnologia de upscaling e IA da Nvidia que permite que jogos como Cyberpunk 2077 e Resident Evil Requiem rodem no pequeno híbrido da Big N. Já o PlayStation 5 Pro se apoia no PSSR 2.0, recurso de upscaling próprio da Sony.
O Series S já consegue rodar jogos pesados, como Crimson Desert, Alan Wake II e Gears of War: E-Day, nativamente, mesmo que com downgrade em comparação com outros consoles. Com o upscaling, o monstrinho pode chegar a outros patamares e até rodar GTA 6 em um nível muito melhor do que esperaríamos inicialmente, embora nem a Microsoft nem a Rockstar tenham revelado se o jogo contará com suporte ao recurso da AMD.
A Microsoft não informou quase nenhum detalhe técnico sobre o FSR 4.1 no XBOX Series, o que abre espaço para especular como o recurso poderá beneficiar os jogos no console.
Resta-nos fazer uma comparação com o desempenho do recurso no PC, já que a AMD liberou o FSR 4.1 para placas RX 6000 antes do tempo. Testes da própria empresa em uma RX 6800 XT conseguiram entregar uma média de 101 FPS em Crimson Desert em 4K, no ultra, com o FSR 4.1 no modo performance e gerador de quadros ligado.
FSR 4.1 chegará a tempo de beneficiar GTA 6?
O anúncio do FSR 4.1 no XBOX aconteceu no dia 20 de outubro, praticamente um mês antes do lançamento de GTA 6. O timing é sugestivo para que a Microsoft implemente a tecnologia nos consoles justamente para receber o jogo da Rockstar 'com a casa arrumada'.
A implementação, no entanto, não tem data definida. O portal Windows Central indica que o recurso de upscaling deve chegar aos consoles até o final de 2026, em um pequeno grupo de jogos otimizados.

candidato.titulo: Scientists shrink Archimedes’ screw to the size of a single molecule
candidato.resumo: Scientists have built a groundbreaking molecular motor that spins in either direction using electricity, inspired by a machine invented more than 2,000 years ago. Even more remarkably, its rotation can boost electrical conductivity by up to 100 times, potentially transforming the future of molecular electronics.

texto_fonte:
Scientists shrink Archimedesâ screw to the size of a single molecule
- Date:
- November 1, 2026
- Source:
- University of Augsburg
- Summary:
- Scientists have built a groundbreaking molecular motor that spins in either direction using electricity, inspired by a machine invented more than 2,000 years ago. Even more remarkably, its rotation can boost electrical conductivity by up to 100 times, potentially transforming the future of molecular electronics.
- Share:
Scientists have developed a remarkable new molecular motor that spins when electricity passes through it. Inspired by an ancient invention, the tiny machine can even reverse its direction when the electrical voltage is switched. The achievement marks an important step toward creating working machines at the smallest possible scale.
Molecular machines are widely seen as a promising next frontier in miniaturization. Nature already provides examples inside living cells, where molecular motors use energy to produce movement. Researchers have spent decades trying to recreate these remarkable biological systems artificially, and progress in this field was recognized with the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
An Ancient Invention Inspires a Molecular Motor
Scientists first developed molecular motors powered directly by electricity in 2011. However, those earlier designs operated on surfaces and relied on the tip of a scanning tunneling microscope to drive their movement.
The new motor takes a different approach, borrowing its basic design from the Archimedes screw, one of the oldest machines in recorded history. Traditionally used to move water uphill, this simple device relies on a rotating spiral to transport material.
Researchers adapted that principle to the molecular scale. Instead of moving water, their design allows electrons to travel through a spiral-shaped molecule, causing it to rotate as electrical current passes through.
A Tiny Molecular Screw Suspended Between Gold Tips
The motor's central component is a specially designed spiral molecule created by the research group of Prof. Michael Pittelkow at the University of Copenhagen. Measuring only a few millionths of a millimeter, the molecule can attach to gold surfaces through sulfur atoms.
At the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, researchers led by Prof. Oren Tal and Dr. Anil Kumar Singh positioned individual molecules between two gold tips sharpened to atomic dimensions. By carefully changing the separation between these electrodes, the team could stretch or compress the molecular screw.
When the scientists applied an electrical voltage, measurements revealed that the molecule began rotating. Even more importantly, they could reverse its direction simply by changing the voltage's polarity.
This represents the first demonstration of a molecular motor that is driven by electrical current, firmly connected to two metal electrodes, and capable of rotating in a controllable direction.
How Electricity Makes a Single Molecule Spin
The driving force comes directly from electrons traveling through the spiral molecule. As they move, they transfer angular momentum to the molecular structure, producing rotation in much the same way that moving air turns a wind turbine.
The spiral's shape determines how it responds to this flow, similar to the difference between screws with right- or left-handed threads. Once the applied voltage exceeds a certain threshold, the movement becomes continuous rotation.
But the experiments revealed another intriguing effect. The rotating molecule conducted electricity much more efficiently than it did when stationary, raising an important question about what was happening inside the tiny machine.
Scientists Discover a Surprising 100-Fold Electrical Effect
To investigate this unexpected behavior, Prof. Dr. Fabian Pauly and his PhD students Léon Martin and Yuta Ito, working at the Chair of Theoretical Physics I at the University of Augsburg, used quantum mechanical simulations on the LiCCA supercomputer.
Their calculations revealed a close relationship between the molecule's rotation and its ability to carry electrical current. Conductivity changes dramatically depending on the angle of the molecule, increasing by as much as two orders of magnitude, or 100 times, during rotation.
The reason turned out to be particularly surprising. Some of the molecular positions that allow electricity to pass most easily are also positions that the molecule naturally avoids when it is not moving. Rotation makes those highly conductive arrangements accessible.
"The surprising thing is that it is precisely the positions that the molecule avoids when at rest that conduct electricity best. It is only the rotation that makes these positions accessible," explains Léon Martin.
The finding demonstrates that molecular motion does more than simply consume electrical energy. The movement itself can strongly influence how electricity flows through the machine.
International Collaboration Solves the Mystery
The researchers then worked with theoretical physicists Per Hedegård of the Niels Bohr Institute in Copenhagen and Jing-Tao Lü of Huazhong University of Science and Technology in Wuhan.
Using the simulation results, the scientists developed a simplified theoretical model that successfully recreated both the rotation observed in the experiments and the accompanying increase in electrical current.
This combination of experimental measurements and theoretical calculations was essential to understanding the mechanism. Although researchers could measure the current passing through the molecule, they needed simulations to determine what was happening at such an extraordinarily small scale.
"In the experiment, you only see the current. Our calculations allow us to glimpse what is happening inside the nanocontact. It was only through close collaboration between experiment and theory across several countries that the mystery of the current increase could be solved," says Yuta Ito, a PhD student originally from Japan.
A New Frontier for Molecular Electronics
The achievement could eventually contribute to the development of molecular electronic components and technologies involving spintronics, which uses properties of electrons beyond their electrical charge. It may also offer possibilities for microfluidic systems, which manipulate extremely small quantities of fluids.
Beyond these potential applications, the motor provides scientists with a new way to investigate physical processes at the atomic scale. Its ability to convert electricity into controlled rotation, while allowing that rotation to influence electrical current, introduces a new principle for designing extraordinarily small machines.
"We have shown that an electric current can be used to generate a directed rotation and that this rotation, in turn, controls the current. This is a new operating principle for machines at the very limits of miniaturization," explains Pauly.
The work at the University of Augsburg received funding from the German Research Foundation (DFG) through Collaborative Research Center (SFB) 1585 (project number 492723217). The computational research was conducted using the University of Augsburg's LiCCA supercomputer (DFG project number 499211671).
Additional support for the collaborating institutions came from the European Research Council (ERC, Horizon 2020, Grant 864008), the Israel Science Foundation (2129/23), the Minerva Foundation, the Villum Foundation, the Novo Nordisk Foundation, the Independent Research Fund Denmark (DFF), the National Key Research and Development Program of China, and the National Natural Science Foundation of China.
